content: The minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of bacteria to antimicrobial compounds should be determined using a standardized procedure. These procedures are based on dilution methods, either broth or agar, or equivalent methods, which utilize standardized inoculum concentrations and standardized concentrations of azithromycin powder. The interpretation of MIC values should follow these criteria: Currently, there is no data available on resistant strains, which prevents the definition of categories other than Susceptible. Strains that yield MIC results indicative of a non-susceptible category should be sent to a reference laboratory for further testing. No interpretive criteria have been established for testing Neisseria gonorrhoeae, as this species is not typically tested. A report of Susceptible indicates that the pathogen is likely to respond to monotherapy with azithromycin. A report of Intermediate suggests that the result is equivocal. If the microorganism is not fully susceptible to alternative, clinically feasible drugs, the test should be repeated. This category implies potential clinical applicability in body sites where the drug is physiologically concentrated or in situations where high drug dosages can be used. It also provides a buffer zone to prevent minor uncontrolled technical factors from causing significant discrepancies in interpretation. A report of Resistant indicates that achievable drug concentrations are unlikely to inhibit the microorganism, and alternative therapy should be selected. Standardized susceptibility test procedures require the use of laboratory control microorganisms to ensure the technical accuracy of the laboratory procedures. Standard azithromycin powder should yield specific MIC values when tested using dilution techniques. Quantitative methods that measure zone diameters also provide reproducible estimates of bacterial susceptibility to antimicrobial compounds. One such standardized procedure involves the use of standardized inoculum concentrations and paper disks impregnated with 15 mcg of azithromycin to test the susceptibility of microorganisms to azithromycin. Laboratory reports providing results from the standardized single-disk susceptibility test with a 15 mcg azithromycin disk should be interpreted as follows: The absence of data on resistant strains precludes defining categories other than Susceptible. Strains yielding zone diameter results indicative of a non-susceptible category should be submitted to a reference laboratory for further testing. No interpretive criteria have been established for testing Neisseria gonorrhoeae, as this species is not routinely tested. Interpretation of results should align with the criteria stated above for dilution techniques. This involves correlating the zone diameter obtained in the disk test with the MIC for azithromycin. As with standardized dilution techniques, diffusion methods require the use of laboratory control microorganisms to ensure the technical accuracy of the procedures. For the diffusion technique, the 15 mcg azithromycin disk should yield specific zone diameters in laboratory test quality control strains. Nonclinical Toxicology There is limited information available regarding the nonclinical toxicology of azithromycin (injection) in the drug label. Clinical Studies No additional details provided in the text. How Supplied Azithromycin for injection is supplied as a white to almost white lyophilized powder under vacuum in a 10-mL vial, equivalent to 500 mg of azithromycin for intravenous administration. It also contains 6 mg of citric acid.
